title: L40S memory budgeting experiments (KV cache + fragmentation + OOM repro)
content:
Doc purpose
- Working log of experiments to stop L40S OOMs + reduce memory-related tail latency jitter during workload-matrix runs.
- Focus: KV cache sizing/budgeting, fragmentation behavior, and “safe by default” guardrails that can ship in the L40S hardware profile.

Background / why this exists
- L40S nodes are cost-effective but much tighter on memory headroom than H100 pools.
- We hit OOMs in perf-suite matrix when long-context + higher concurrency + streaming overlap.
- Pattern: stable for ~5–20 minutes, then sudden OOM after a few “bad” requests (long prefill + uneven decode lengths) and memory doesn’t recover.

Assumptions / test setup (keep honest)
- GPU: NVIDIA L40S 48GB (PCIe). Driver/CUDA versions varied by runner pool; recorded per run.
- Runtime branch: profile-pack feature branch (pre-merge) + a couple runs on main for baseline.
- Models: mix from workload matrix; emphasis on “long prompt” and “tool-ish / JSON-ish output” prompts because they create spiky decode patterns.
- Quantization: mostly off for these tests (to isolate KV/cache + allocator behavior). One quick sanity run with 4-bit to see if the failure mode changes.
- Scheduler: continuous batching ON in all runs; we only changed queue limits and per-request token caps when explicitly noted.
- Observability: collected per-process GPU alloc, “reserved vs used”, runtime KV cache stats (when available), and request-level p95.

Terminology / knobs referenced (current runtime naming; may change)
- KV cache: memory used to store K/V tensors per layer for each active sequence.
- “Budget”: an explicit cap on how much GPU memory we’ll allow KV cache to occupy before we start rejecting/queuing/downsizing.
- “Headroom”: memory reserved for model weights, activation scratch, comms buffers, etc.
- Fragmentation: inability to satisfy a large allocation despite “free” memory existing (holes).

Quick symptom summary (what we saw repeatedly)
1) Long-context + medium concurrency causes KV growth during prefill.
2) After some churn (requests ending, new ones starting), reserved memory creeps up.
3) Eventually a new prefill triggers a large contiguous allocation; allocator can’t find it; OOM.
4) After OOM, worker restarts => perf-canary noise + customers would see elevated 5xx.

Run log (chronological-ish)

Run L40S-EXP-001 (baseline, no KV budgeting)
- Date: 2025-11-27
- Runner: l40s-perf-06 (note: this runner also had intermittent perf-canary flakiness; see INT-8832)
- Workload slice: long-context bucket + streaming
- Result: OOM within ~18 min
- Notes:
  - OOM typically during prefill (not decode).
  - GPU “free” reported >2GB right before crash, but large alloc fails.
  - Suggests fragmentation or sudden scratch spike.

Run L40S-EXP-002 (reduce max concurrent sequences, keep batching)
- Date: 2025-11-28
- Change: lower max_concurrent_seqs from baseline setting (baseline was tuned for H100-ish throughput)
- Result: OOM moved out to ~42 min, still reproducible
- Tradeoff: throughput down; p95 improved slightly (less queue thrash)
- Notes:
  - This is a lever, but we’d rather not rely purely on low concurrency; we need deterministic guardrails.

Run L40S-EXP-003 (hard cap KV cache budget)
- Date: 2025-11-29
- Change: set KV cache budget to ~60–65% of total GPU memory (targeting ~28–31GB KV)
- Result: no OOM in 90 min run; saw controlled backpressure instead
- Behavior:
  - When budget approached, scheduler started queueing/rejecting (depending on mode) before OOM.
  - p95 got worse in the highest concurrency segment (expected), but errors were “clean” (429/over-cap) vs process OOM.
- Notes:
  - This is the first run that “felt shippable”: predictable degradation.
  - Need to ensure the fallback mode is correct (queue vs reject) depending on Hosted vs Dedicated.

Run L40S-EXP-004 (KV budget too aggressive)
- Date: 2025-11-30
- Change: KV budget ~45–50% of GPU
- Result: stable, but throughput tanked; too much throttling
- Notes:
  - Customers will perceive this as “L40S is slow” rather than “L40S is cost-effective.”
  - Keep this as emergency mode only.

Run L40S-EXP-005 (KV budget + reserved headroom for scratch)
- Date: 2025-12-01
- Change: KV budget ~60% + explicit headroom reserve (attempt to avoid prefill scratch spikes)
- Result: stable; best p95 among stable runs
- Notes:
  - Prefill spikes appear less likely to cross the cliff.
  - We should document headroom assumptions (weights + runtime scratch + fragmentation cushion).

Run L40S-EXP-006 (fragmentation stress: mixed seq lengths)
- Date: 2025-12-02
- Workload slice: interleave short + long prompts; high churn
- Result: without budgeting OOM; with budgeting stable but saw “reserved memory creep” still.
- Observations:
  - Even when KV budget holds, reserved memory didn’t fully return to baseline after churn.
  - Hypothesis: allocator caching + block reuse patterns; not necessarily a leak, but effectively reduced usable headroom.

Run L40S-EXP-007 (attempt: change KV block size / paging granularity)
- Date: 2025-12-03
- Change: larger KV blocks => fewer alloc calls, but worse internal fragmentation; smaller blocks => more overhead but smoother.
- Result: smaller blocks reduced OOM frequency in no-budget runs but didn’t eliminate; with budgeting both were fine.
- Notes:
  - Probably not worth locking block size in profile unless we can prove low risk across models.
  - If we ship one change: ship budget + concurrency/queue defaults; keep block-size adaptive.

Run L40S-EXP-008 (quantized model sanity check)
- Date: 2025-12-04
- Change: enable quantization variant for one model family
- Result: more headroom helps, but OOM still possible without budgeting under churn.
- Conclusion: budget/guardrails still required; quantization isn’t a substitute.

What “fragmentation” looked like in practice (notes, not proofs)
- We saw OOM with >1–3GB “free” reported (depending on tool) right before crash.
- OOM often triggered by a larger contiguous allocation during prefill (or a temporary buffer) rather than KV growth alone.
- After long runs, “reserved” stayed high even when active sequences dropped.
- Two likely contributors:
  1) Allocation pattern from mixed seq lengths (start/stop) causing holes.
  2) CUDA allocator caching behavior + runtime memory pools holding onto blocks.
- Actionable: leave a larger safety cushion on L40S than on H100; enforce KV ceiling earlier.

OOM repro steps (for debugging / CI repro attempts)
Goal: reproduce on a single worker in <30 minutes.

Repro recipe A (most reliable so far)
1) Use L40S worker, clean restart.
2) Enable continuous batching.
3) Set high-ish concurrency (enough to keep 8–16 sequences active; exact number depends on model).
4) Send a repeating mix:
   - 30% short prompts (few hundred tokens prompt, short decode)
   - 50% medium prompts (1–2k prompt, moderate decode)
   - 20% long prompts (8–16k prompt, streaming decode)
5) Keep arrival rate slightly above steady-state throughput so queues form.
6) Run 15–30 minutes.
Expected: reserved memory creeps up; eventually an OOM during a long prefill.

Repro recipe B (prefill spike)
1) Pre-warm with short traffic for 5 minutes.
2) Then burst 5–10 long prompts concurrently (same model).
3) Repeat every 2 minutes.
Expected: OOM occurs earlier; looks like “large prefill scratch + existing KV footprint.”

Data to capture when OOM happens (oncall / dev)
- Effective runtime config dump (see redwood/pr-22066 tool) including:
  - selected hardware profile
  - KV budget values
  - concurrency limits
  - queue limits / backpressure mode
- GPU memory snapshot (used/reserved) + active seq count + KV blocks allocated
- The 10 requests leading up to crash: prompt len, max_new_tokens, streaming on/off
- Any allocator warnings in logs

Proposed guardrails (candidate L40S profile defaults)
These are draft numbers; we need to translate to exact runtime keys.

1) KV cache budget (primary)
- Default: cap KV cache to ~60–65% of total GPU memory on L40S.
- Rationale: keeps ~35–40% for weights + scratch + fragmentation cushion.
- Behavior when exceeded:
  - Prefer backpressure (queue) in Dedicated/Private when possible.
  - Prefer controlled rejection (429 / “capacity”) in Hosted to protect fleet stability.

2) Concurrency + queue defaults (secondary)
- Lower max_concurrent_seqs vs H100 defaults.
- Set max_queue_depth and/or max_queue_tokens to prevent “infinite waiting” + memory churn.
- Use fairness settings that avoid prefill starvation but do not explode tail latency.

3) Request-level safety
- Enforce max_prompt_tokens (or route long-context workloads to appropriate pools).
- For streaming: cap max_new_tokens in public tiers (product decision, but impacts stability directly).

4) Headroom reservation
- Explicitly reserve a fixed minimum headroom (GB) or percent so transient scratch allocations don’t hit the cliff.

5) Debuggability
- Ensure L40S profile emits explicit log lines: KV budget, headroom, and what triggered throttling.
- Metric: “kv_budget_exceeded_count” (or similar) so SRE can see we’re throttling instead of silently degrading.

Open questions / TODO
- What’s the right default for “degrade mode”: queue vs reject, per deployment mode?
- How much does driver/CUDA version change allocator behavior on L40S runners? (we saw variance; need controlled A/B).
- Can we reduce reserved-memory creep by tuning allocator settings globally, or is that too risky for profile pack?
- Do we want different L40S profiles for 48GB vs any smaller variants (if they exist in partner fleets)?

Next steps
- Align proposed KV budget + headroom defaults with Sofia/Lena (scheduler), Samir (memory), and SRE guardrails.
- Feed these defaults into ENG-4825 and ensure they’re encoded in the profile pack + validated by schema.
- Add a perf-canary gate specifically for “OOM-free for X minutes under churn workload slice” on L40S.
- Update the Known Issues page with:
  - “long-context + churn on L40S can OOM without KV budgeting”
  - Mitigation: enable L40S profile, reduce concurrency, enforce prompt caps

Notes to self (don’t ship as promises)
- We should be careful in docs: L40S profile is about stability and predictable behavior, not “it will always be faster.”
- The win here is avoiding hard OOM and swapping in controlled backpressure.
- Also: keep wording consistent with the “expected behavior” doc guidance (see docs Slack thread on guarantees).
